book.title: Sefer Luḳov : geheyliḳṭ der ḥorev-geṿorener ḳehile

overview.title: Reading Jewish Łuków through Sefer Lukov
overview.summary: Łuków was home to a longstanding Jewish community whose religious life, schools, libraries, newspapers, political movements, businesses, and families shaped the town. The memorial book traces this world from earlier settlement and communal institutions through wartime occupation, ghettoization, murder, deportation, hiding, resistance, and survival. Its testimonies also show how survivors and descendants rebuilt community memory after the Holocaust. By following the paths below, readers can understand both the richness of Jewish Łuków before the destruction and the human choices, losses, and acts of remembrance recorded afterward.

paths.title: How long had Jewish Łuków existed, and what held the community together?
paths.description: This path establishes Łuków’s historical depth and introduces the institutions, religious authorities, and communal rights that sustained Jewish life. By the end, readers will see the community not as a prelude to catastrophe, but as a society with its own history and structures.
paths.question: What made Jewish Łuków a community before the Holocaust?

steps.title: A community with deep roots
steps.summary: The memorial book places an early settlement in Łuków in the twelfth century, identifies the town’s establishment in 1230, and records its official recognition as a town in 1403. It also preserves population records of 911 Jewish poll-tax payers in 1765 and 1,877 Jews in 1840, showing a community with a long and documented presence.

steps.title: Religious learning as lived experience
steps.summary: The records connect Łuków with rabbinic figures and works including the Bayit Hadash, Ketoret HaSamim, and Tevuot Shor, while personal recollections describe prayer, study, bar mitzvah, and communal observance. Together, these accounts show religious life as both scholarship and everyday practice.

paths.title: What did modern Jewish life look like in Łuków?
paths.description: This path follows the growth of education, Yiddish culture, youth movements, and political debate from the early twentieth century. It shows how Łuków’s Jews created competing but interconnected visions of communal life.
paths.question: How did education, culture, and politics shape younger generations?

steps.title: Schools for different communities and needs
steps.summary: The Medem folk school opened in October 1928, while Tsisho education primarily served children from poor working-class families. Beit Yaakov offered girls’ schooling, and students’ secret attendance at Hashomer Hatzair activities reveals tensions between established religious education and new youth movements.

paths.title: How did families and work organize everyday life?
paths.description: This path reconstructs Łuków through workplaces, shops, streets, and family histories preserved in the book. It helps readers understand the community as an interconnected economy and neighborhood network before occupation destroyed those relationships.
paths.question: Where did people work, trade, live, and raise families?

steps.title: Factories and skilled work
steps.summary: The Gastman mechanical shoe factory moved from Warsaw to Łuków in 1906–1907 and is described as employing 300 workers. Other records recall Lieberman’s album factory, brass workshops, mills, bakeries, printing, barbering, and sewing-machine sales, revealing a varied Jewish working and commercial life.

paths.title: How did occupation transform Łuków into a site of persecution and murder?
paths.description: This path follows the escalation from war and occupation to ghetto rule, shootings, Aktionen, deportation, and the destruction of families. It keeps the memorial book’s testimony at the center while identifying the people and institutions involved in these events.
paths.question: What happened to Łuków’s Jews under occupation?

steps.title: War and German occupation
steps.summary: The memorial book describes the catastrophe beginning with the German invasion of Poland in September 1939 and refers to Łuków’s transformation during the occupation. It also records a Judenrat headed by Weintraub during the first period of German rule, marking the forced reorganization of communal life under persecution.

paths.title: How did people resist, survive, and remember?
paths.description: This path traces clandestine political activity, escapes, hiding, armed resistance, and the postwar work of rebuilding memory. It shows survival as a mixture of courage, mutual aid, chance, and painful return—not a simple ending to the story.
paths.question: What forms did resistance and survival take, and how was Łuków remembered afterward?

steps.title: Resistance inside and beyond the ghetto
steps.summary: The book recalls a clandestine gathering commemorating the Great October Revolution and describes Reuben Heyblum’s underground work sending medicines to partisan detachments. Nahum Goldzak is remembered as a Łuków-born activist who aided underground resistance and later became a partisan survivor.

steps.title: Memory as communal reconstruction
steps.summary: The Łuków landsmanschaft in Brussels, memorial evenings for ghetto victims, survivor publications, and the Yizkor book itself became forms of communal remembrance. These efforts preserved names, testimonies, cultural life, and the claim that Jewish Łuków should be known as a living community as well as a destroyed one.

timeline.title: Modern communal life expands
timeline.summary: The period saw workers’ activity and secret Bundist organization, the relocation of Gastman’s shoe factory to Łuków, the founding of a library, political parties, city council elections, and a Bund cooperative shop. Relief from New York and the Joint also connected local life to wider Jewish networks.
